editorNote: Dial-up networks answer intruders with new hardware while Atari rebuilds its home-computer line and Lucasfilm prepares a new kind of computer game.
morningLine: The telephone line is becoming both the personal computer’s doorway and its newest lock.

lead.headline: Telenet Locks the Dial-Up Door
lead.dek: A new device promises to bar unauthorized callers from computer systems reached over telephone lines.
body: WASHINGTON — GTE Telenet introduced a device Tuesday, May 15, designed to lock unauthorized users out of computer systems reached through telephone lines. The announcement turns the fast-growing worry over modem intrusion into a commercial hardware market.

Dial-up access is spreading beyond large institutions as lower-priced modems bring telecommunications within reach of homes and small offices. That convenience also means a computer can have a doorway far beyond the machine room, and network operators are now selling a lock for it.

The period report does not name a hacker crew or connect the product to a particular break-in. Its significance is broader: access control has become a product category, proof that remote computing is mature enough to demand both openness and defenses.

For home users, the same week’s magazine racks advertise comparisons of six modems below $100. The modem is moving from specialist equipment toward a mass-market peripheral just as the networks at the other end learn to question who is calling.

stories.headline: Atari Pledges a Sober XL Comeback
body: After a half-billion-dollar loss in 1983, Atari says its recovery will rest on profitability, reliability and products customers actually want. Chief executive James Morgan’s program includes a 40 percent overhead reduction and fewer premature promises.
The 600XL and 800XL are cast as the workhorses. A roughly $100 model 1064 module can expand the 16K 600XL to 64K, while specifications for the ambitious 1450XLD remain under review.
Software is part of the repair job: SynFile+, SynCalc and SynTrend, acquired from Synapse, bring database, spreadsheet, graphing and statistics tools to Atari’s 8-bit line at $99.95 each.

stories.headline: Lucasfilm Turns Its Cameras Toward Games
body: George Lucas’s company has entered the home video-game market, bringing film-production talent into interactive entertainment. The May 8 announcement was still fresh as this week began.

The venture stresses original play rather than a simple movie license. Its first Atari-computer projects would become Ballblazer, a futuristic split-screen sport, and Rescue on Fractalus!, a tense flight across an alien landscape.

stories.headline: Sub-$100 Modems Call the Home Office
body: The May issue of Computers & Electronics puts six modems costing less than $100 on its cover, a vivid sign that data communications is crossing a consumer price threshold.

Micro-to-mainframe access, bulletin boards and online services are becoming practical ambitions for a household machine. The bargain modem expands the audience—and makes the week’s Telenet security announcement feel less remote.
